 1                  MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
 2   I.       INTRODUCTION
 3            In this putative nationwide class action, Plaintiffs allege American Airlines,
 4   Inc. (“American”) breached a contract regarding its frequent flyer program (called
 5   AAdvantage) that is governed by Texas law, based upon actions that American took
 6   in Fort Worth, Texas. The Northern District of Texas, Fort Worth Division, is the
 7   natural forum for the resolution of this dispute. And while a plaintiff’s choice of
 8   forum always weighs against transfer, the named Plaintiffs’ choice of forum is
 9   entitled to considerably less weight here, where six of the eight named Plaintiffs’
10   claims have no nexus to this jurisdiction, and thus would need to be dismissed for
11   lack of personal jurisdiction unless the case is transferred. (See Dkt. No. 17.)
12            Several additional reasons support transfer. Plaintiffs’ lawsuit is based on the
13   termination of putative class members’ AAdvantage accounts based on findings of
14   fraud and abuse. Before American made those decisions, it individually reviewed
15   the facts and circumstances relating to each AAdvantage account. Those reviews
16   and decisions were made by individuals living and working in Texas, where both
17   the documentary evidence and key witnesses are located. Further, the merits of this
18   case are governed by Texas law, which the federal courts in Texas are more
19   frequently called upon to apply, and time to trial in the Northern District of Texas is
20   almost half what it is here. Accordingly, transfer furthers the interests of both
21   convenience and justice.
22            Accordingly, American respectfully requests that the Court transfer venue
23   pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
24   II.      STATEMENT OF FACTS
25            Four of the named Plaintiffs currently reside in this District, yet only two
26   resided in this District at the time their claims arose—i.e., when their AAdvantage
27   accounts were terminated. (FAC ¶¶ 54, 80, 98, 125.) The other four Plaintiffs
28   reside in Michigan and Connecticut. (Id. ¶¶ 148, 166, 182, 204.) All of the
                                                                   MOTION TO TRANSFER VENUE
                                            -1-                              5:24-CV-00530-PCP
        Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 20 Filed 03/06/24 Page 5 of 12



 1   Plaintiffs claims arise from the termination of their memberships in American’s
 2   frequent flyer program—AAdvantage—based upon findings by American that the
 3   named Plaintiffs and putative class members engaged in fraud and abuse of the
 4   program. (FAC ¶ 236.) Those decisions were made by analysts working at
 5   American’s headquarters in the Northern District of Texas. (Declaration of Miki
 6   Rezentes (“Rezentes Decl.”) ¶¶ 2, 4.) The relevant decisionmakers are thus in Fort
 7   Worth, where American has its principal place of business. (Id.) Six analysts
 8   responsible for the termination decisions are still American employees and work for
 9   American at its Fort Worth headquarters. (Id. ¶ 4.) Two—James Blake and
10   Jennifer Tucker—are no longer American employees, and they too reside within the
11   Northern District of Texas. (Id.)
12          In addition to the analysts who conducted the fact investigations related to
13   the individual members’ accounts and an employee who assisted them, the
14   employees responsible for overseeing the AAdvantage program and its program
15   partnerships (including American’s relationship with Citi and Barclays), are also
16   potential witnesses. Four such individuals no longer work for American: Chelsea
17   Casiano, who held the role of Senior Analyst – AAdvantage Product Expert;
18   Bridget Blaise-Shamai, who held the role of President of the AAdvantage Program;
19   Janet Ferguson, who held the role of Director of AAdvantage Customer Service;
20   and Neva Ignatow, who held the role of Director of Domestic Program
21   Partnerships. (Id. ¶¶ 5–7.) These potential witnesses all reside within the Northern
22   District of Texas. (Id.) By contrast, American is unaware of any essential third-
23   party witnesses who reside in this District or relevant documentary evidence that
24   would be located here.
25   III.   ARGUMENT
26          28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) governs motions to transfer and states: “For the
27   convenience of parties and witnesses, in the interest of justice, a district court may
28   transfer any civil action to any other district or division where it might have been
                                                                 MOTION TO TRANSFER VENUE
                                          -2-                              5:24-CV-00530-PCP
        Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 20 Filed 03/06/24 Page 6 of 12



 1   brought or to any district or division to which the parties have consented.”
 2           This action could have been brought in the Northern District of Texas. The
 3   Northern District of Texas would have subject matter jurisdiction over this action
 4   under the Class Action Fairness Act for the same reasons as this Court. (FAC
 5   ¶ 11.) The Northern District of Texas—unlike this Court—can exercise general
 6   jurisdiction over American because American’s principal place of business is
 7   located there. (Rezentes Decl. ¶ 2.) And venue is proper in the Northern District of
 8   Texas because American resides there, and a substantial part of the events giving
 9   rise to the claims occurred there. (Id. ¶¶ 3–9.)
10           “A motion to transfer venue under § 1404(a)” then “requires the court to
11   weigh multiple factors in its determination whether transfer is appropriate in a
12   particular case. For example, the court may consider: (1) the location where the
13   relevant agreements were negotiated and executed, (2) the state that is most familiar
14   with the governing law, (3) the plaintiff’s choice of forum, (4) the respective
15   parties’ contacts with the forum, (5) the contacts relating to the plaintiff’s cause of
16   action in the chosen forum, (6) the differences in the costs of litigation in the two
17   forums, (7) the availability of compulsory process to compel attendance of
18   unwilling non-party witnesses, and (8) the ease of access to sources of proof.”
19   Jones v. GNC Franchising, Inc., 211 F.3d 495, 498-99 (9th Cir. 2000). The factors
20   are not exclusive, and not every factor will weigh heavily in the outcome of each
21   case.
22           Here, the overwhelming majority of these factors—including the availability
23   of compulsory process to compel attendance of non-party witnesses, which is
24   typically considered the most important factor—favor transfer.
25           1.    The Contract At Issue Was Drafted In Texas.
26           The first Jones factor favors transfer. Where, as here, the parties were not all
27   in the same physical location for the negotiation and execution of the contracts,
28   courts look to where the agreement was drafted. See, e.g., Inherent.com v.
                                                                  MOTION TO TRANSFER VENUE
                                           -3-                              5:24-CV-00530-PCP
          Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 20 Filed 03/06/24 Page 7 of 12



 1   Martindale-Hubbell, 420 F. Supp. 2d 1093, 1102 (N.D. Cal. 2006); Vernon v.
 2   Qwest Communications Int’l, Inc., 643 F. Supp. 2d 1256, 1270 (W.D. Wash. 2009).
 3   Here, the Terms and Conditions governing American’s AAdvantage program
 4   constitute the relevant agreement, and American drafted those Terms and
 5   Conditions in Texas. (Rezentes Decl. ¶ 3.) Thus, this factor weighs in favor of
 6   transfer.
 7           2.     Texas Courts Are Most Familiar With The Governing Law.
 8           The second Jones factor—which state is most familiar with the governing
 9   law—also favors transfer. The contract on which Plaintiffs’ case is based is
10   governed by Texas law. (Id.) Each version of the Terms and Conditions in effect
11   at all relevant times in this litigation contained a Texas choice-of-law provision.
12   (Id.) Federal courts in Texas are likely to be more familiar than this Court with
13   Texas contract law. 1
14           3.     Plaintiffs’ Choice Of Forum Should Be Afforded Little Weight.
15           The next Jones factor, the Plaintiffs’ choice of forum, always weighs against
16   transfer. But it is entitled to less weight here for two reasons. First, Plaintiffs seek
17   to represent a nationwide class of individuals who did not choose this forum. See
18   Lou v. Belzberg, 834 F.2d 730, 739 (9th Cir. 1987) (“when an individual brings a
19   derivative suit or represents a class, the named plaintiff’s choice of forum is given
20   less weight”) (citation omitted).
21           Second, six of eight named Plaintiffs cannot even bring suit here—and
22   obviously, a court should not defer to a plaintiff’s decision to sue in a forum that
23   cannot hear the claim. (See Dkt. No. 17.) The claims brought by Derrick
24   Gallagher, Abigail Gallagher, Eric Link, Miranda Link, Elliot Weiner, Rachel Feit
25   1

26   (FAC ¶¶ 261-69.) But for the reasons explained in American’s concurrently-filed motion to
     dismiss, Plaintiffs’ state-law claim for unjust enrichment is preempted by the Airline
27   Deregulation Act (“ADA”). (See Dkt. No. 17.) Indeed, as explained in American’s motion to
     dismiss, the only claim that Plaintiffs can actually assert in this action is a breach of contract
28   claim, and Plaintiffs’ breach of contract claim is governed by Texas law. (See id.)

 1   do not arise out of or relate to American’s contacts here. (See id. at 5.) Unless the
 2   case is transferred, three quarters of the named Plaintiffs’ claims will need to be
 3   dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction. If anything, transfer would benefit the
 4   named Plaintiffs (by saving their claims), while allowing this Court to avoid this
 5   jurisdictional issue. And it would benefit the putative class: it would ensure that
 6   the court considering class certification can choose among eight named Plaintiffs,
 7   thus affording the putative class the chance at “the best possible representation.”
 8   China Agritech v. Resh, 584 U.S. 732, 740 (2018) (quotations omitted).
 9         4.     The Parties Have Greater Contacts With Texas.
10         The fourth Jones factor—the respective parties’ contacts with the forum—
11   likewise favors transfer. Only half of the named Plaintiffs currently reside in this
12   forum (FAC ¶¶ 2-9), and most of the putative class members they seek to represent
13   have no particular contacts with this forum. Such circumstances favor transfer. See
14   Roberts v. CR England, Inc., 827 F. Supp. 2d 1078, 1087 (N.D. Cal. 2011) (“On
15   balance, the fourth factor — the parties’ respective contacts with the forum — also
16   favors Utah. Defendants have greater contacts with Utah, where they are
17   headquartered. Although Roberts and McKay live in California, they seek to
18   represent a nationwide class of drivers, many of whom may not have had contact
19   with this district, but likely have had contact with Utah.”); Saunders v. USAA Life
20   Ins. Co., 71 F. Supp. 3d 1058, 1061 (N.D. Cal. 2014) (“The Fourth and fifth factors
21   favor transfer because Defendant has little connection with California outside of the
22   presence of policyholders in this state, and all of the conduct underlying the
23   premium increase occurred in Texas.”).
24         5.     The Parties Have Greater Relevant Contacts With Texas.
25         The fifth Jones factor—the respective parties’ contacts related to the
26   Plaintiffs’ cause of action with the forum—even more strongly favors transfer.
27   Plaintiffs allege that American “maintained a base in this District located at the San
28   Francisco International Airport,” and “Plaintiffs used their miles in their
                                                                 MOTION TO TRANSFER VENUE
                                          -5-                              5:24-CV-00530-PCP
        Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 20 Filed 03/06/24 Page 9 of 12



 1   AAdvantage accounts for flights departing from and arriving at airports in this
 2   District.” (FAC ¶ 12.) But Plaintiffs’ claims do not relate to flights operated by
 3   American in and out of San Francisco. Plaintiffs’ claims arise out of the alleged
 4   “wrongful and unilateral termination of AAdvantage accounts, resulting in the loss
 5   of airline miles benefits that had been accrued based on previous purchases.” (FAC
 6   ¶ 1.) American employees in Texas made the relevant termination decisions.
 7   (Rezentes Decl. ¶¶ 4, 8.) Thus, even to the extent that the parties have some
 8   contacts with this forum, the parties’ relevant contacts are all with Texas—not here.
 9         The court reached a similar conclusion in Hoefert v. American Airlines Inc.,
10   No. CV-17-02996-PHX-SPL, 2018 WL 2740276 (D. Ariz. June 7, 2018). There,
11   “the Plaintiff argue[d] that the Defendant transacts business in the forum because of
12   its flight operations at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport located in Phoenix,
13   Arizona.” Id. at *2. But the court in transferring the action noted that “[t]he
14   majority of the events giving rise to this litigation were based in operations and
15   actions that took place in Fort Worth, Texas.” Id. at *3; see also Chen v. Pioneer
16   Oil, LLC, 472 F. Supp. 3d 704, 709 (N.D. Cal. 2020) (“While Pioneer Oil has
17   business contacts in the Northern District of California, Chen does not allege that
18   any of the challenged conduct occurred here.”) (citation omitted). That is equally
19   true here.
20         6.     Litigation Would Be More Efficient In Texas.
21         The sixth Jones factor—the differences in the costs of litigation in the two
22   forums—favors transfer. “Generally, litigation costs are reduced when venue is
23   located near the most witnesses expected to testify.” Park v. Dole Fresh
24   Vegetables, Inc., 964 F. Supp. 2d 1088, 1095 (N.D. Cal. 2013). Here, the current
25   and former American employees with information relevant to this dispute are
26   located within the Northern District of Texas. (Rezentes Decl. ¶¶ 4–7.) There are
27   at least 12 such witnesses who reside in Texas. (Id.) By contrast, while four of the
28   eight named Plaintiffs reside here, the other four do not, and the nationwide class
                                                                 MOTION TO TRANSFER VENUE
                                          -6-                              5:24-CV-00530-PCP
          Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 20 Filed 03/06/24 Page 10 of 12



 1   that they seek to represent is located throughout the country. (FAC ¶¶ 2–9, 236.)
 2   In such circumstances, courts have noted that a more central location can reduce
 3   costs. See Roberts, 827 F. Supp. 2d at 1087 (“The sixth factor, the costs of
 4   litigation, appears to favor transfer” where the named plaintiffs “and certain drivers
 5   and witnesses live in California” but “[t]he remaining drivers live in locations
 6   throughout the United States. Utah is more centrally located than this district.”).
 7           Further, the most recent Federal Court Management Statistics published by
 8   the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts on behalf of the Federal Judiciary,
 9   show that this Court faces a significantly higher caseload, with significantly longer
10   times to trial, than the Northern District of Texas. See Fed. Ct. Mgmt.
11   Stats.−Profiles, U.S. Courts (Dec. 31, 2023), available at
12   https://www.uscourts.gov/statistics/table/na/federal-court-management-
13   statistics/2023/12/31-1 (last visited February 25, 2024). The median time from
14   filing to trial for civil cases in the Northern District of Texas is 27.3 months, with
15   11.1% of civil cases remaining on the docket for over three years. Id. By contrast,
16   the median time from filing to trial for civil cases in the Northern District of
17   California is 48.9 months, with 21.7% of civil cases remaining on the docket for
18   over three years. Id. Thus, this case could proceed more efficiently in the Northern
19   District of Texas, at a lower cost, and with a lower burden on this Court and the
20   local jury pool. 2
21           7.    Non-Party Witnesses Can Be Compelled To Testify In Texas.
22           The seventh Jones factor—the availability of compulsory process to compel
23   attendance of unwilling non-party witnesses—strongly favors transfer. Indeed, this
24   factor is generally considered the most important. See generally Park, 964 F. Supp.
25

28   not surprising that the time to trial is nearly twice as long.

11   797, 800 (9th Cir. 2004). In assessing whether a defendant is subject to personal
12   jurisdiction, courts engage in a two-pronged inquiry—(1) whether personal
13   jurisdiction is permitted under the forum state’s long-arm statute; and (2) whether
14   personal jurisdiction complies with constitutional due process. See Williams v.
15   Yamaha Motor Co., 851 F.3d 1015, 1020 (9th Cir. 2017) (citing Fed. R. Civ. P.
16   4(k)(1)(A)). California authorizes its courts to exercise personal jurisdiction “to the
17   full extent that such exercise comports with due process.” Id. (citing Cal. Civ.
18   Proc. Code § 410.10). Accordingly, “the jurisdictional analyses under California
19   state law and federal due process are the same.’” Axiom Foods, Inc. v. Acerchem
20   Int’l, Inc., 874 F.3d 1064, 1067 (9th Cir. 2017) (brackets and quotations omitted).

13   typically considered “at home” only where it is incorporated or has its principal
14   place of business. Id. at 137; AM Trust v. UBS AG, 681 F. App’x 587, 588 (9th Cir.
15   2017). “This is an exacting standard, as it should be, because a finding of general

26         Congress enacted the ADA “[t]o ensure that the States would not undo
27   federal deregulation” of the airline industry. Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc.,
28   504 U.S. 374, 378 (1992). The ADA’s express purpose is “to leave largely to

 6   services.’” Morales, 504 U.S. at 378 (citation, quotations, brackets, and ellipses
 7   omitted).
 8         The ADA includes a preemption clause providing that a state “may not enact
 9   or enforce a law, regulation, or other provision having the force and effect of law
10   related to a price, route, or service of an air carrier.” 49 U.S.C. § 41713. The
11   phrase “relating to” is “a broad one—‘to stand in some relation; to have bearing or
12   concern; to pertain; refer; to bring into association with or connection with’—and
13   the words thus express a broad pre-emptive purpose.” Morales, 504 U.S. at 383
14   (internal citation omitted). Any state law claim “having a connection with or
15   reference to airline rates, routes, or services” is preempted under the ADA. Id. at
16   384 (internal quotations omitted). The Supreme Court has twice reaffirmed the
17   ADA’s “broad preemptive purpose.” See Wolens, 513 U.S. at 228–29; Northwest,
18   Inc. v. Ginsberg, 572 U.S. 273, 280 (2014). All such state laws are preempted as
19   applied to air carriers—including laws of general application, not just those that are
20   specific to air carriers. In Morales, for example, the Supreme Court held that the
21   ADA preempts state-law consumer protection statutes prohibiting deceptive
22   advertising, when those statutes are applied to air fare advertising and frequent flyer
23   programs. Id. at 387–90. In doing so, the Supreme Court rejected as “utterly
24   irrational” the “notion that only state laws specifically addressed to the airline
25   industry are pre-empted.” Id. at 386.

27   contract claims “seeking recovery solely for the airline’s alleged breach of its own,
28   self-imposed undertakings.” Wolens, 513 U.S. at 228. There, the plaintiffs (like

26   good faith and fair dealing.” Id. at 281. The Court had “little difficulty rejecting
27   this argument. To begin, state common-law rules fall comfortably within the
28   language of the ADA pre-emption provision.” Id. “Exempting common-law
